titulo.texto: The Closed Rooms: The Secret Wardrobe

frase_gancho.texto: Diego Rivera asked that his bathroom be kept closed for fifteen years. It was opened much later.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the first display case, where the corsets that Frida painted are kept.

guion_corto.texto: This hall exists thanks to a closed door. Diego Rivera asked Dolores Olmedo, a friend of his, to keep his bathroom closed for fifteen years. Olmedo also closed the bathroom of Frida’s bedroom, a storeroom, trunks and drawers. Inside were dresses, corsets, medicines, toys, books, photographs and thousands of documents. In the year two thousand four, the museum began to open everything. Cataloging the material took almost three years. Close to three hundred items of clothing turned up, along with unexpected things, such as a drawing hidden behind some books. What you see in these display cases came out of those rooms. Today you can see part of that wardrobe.

guion_largo.texto:
Some of the most important things in this house were kept away for decades. When Frida died, in nineteen fifty-four, Diego Rivera stored many of her belongings in his own bathroom. He asked Dolores Olmedo, a friend of his, to keep it closed for fifteen years. Diego died in nineteen fifty-seven.

Olmedo did something more. She also kept closed the bathroom of Frida’s bedroom, a storeroom, trunks, wardrobes and drawers. Diego had left a brief inventory of the things he stored in his bathroom. Everything else remained in the dark. The spaces stayed closed for many years after that deadline.

In the year two thousand four, the museum began to open them. Hilda Trujillo, director of the museum since two thousand two, recalls that it was then that they began to open everything. What turned up was enormous. Work lasting almost three years, with support from the ADABI association, made it possible to catalog the material. There were twenty-two thousand one hundred five documents, five thousand three hundred eighty-seven photographs, three thousand eight hundred seventy-four magazines and two thousand seven hundred seventy-six books. There were also drawings, personal objects, dresses, corsets, medicines and toys. Among the items of clothing, there are about three hundred.

The findings included surprises. A drawing from Frida’s notebook, called Las apariencias engañan, turned up hidden behind some books in a closet. Some drafts confirmed that Frida herself wrote a text about Diego that for years had been attributed to Alfonso Reyes.

With that material, an exhibition was prepared and called Las apariencias engañan, los vestidos de Frida Kahlo. It was presented at the Casa Azul and then traveled to other countries. It was shown at the De Young in San Francisco, at the Brooklyn Museum and at the Drents Museum. In London, the Victoria and Albert presented another show with part of that material. The show fills five rooms and brings together nearly three hundred items of clothing, as well as jewelry, corsets and orthopedic devices.

Now think about what the title means. Appearances can be deceiving. Frida used her clothing to present herself. But beneath the long skirts, the huipiles and the rebozos, there were corsets and devices that supported her. What was shown and what was hidden were part of the same story.

This hall preserves a part of that wardrobe, and the selection may change with each exhibition. It is usually dimly lit, because light damages old fabrics.

When you enter, think that all of this was stored, in the dark, for years. Now you can see it, and that too is part of the story of the house.

texto.pregunta: Myth: The dresses and corsets in this hall were always part of the museum’s tour.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were stored in closed spaces for decades. The museum began to open them in two thousand four, and the exhibition of her wardrobe was later presented at the Casa Azul and in other countries.
